query: Contract asset vs notes receivable in T's rev rec installment programs.
rag_answer: In T's revenue recognition for installment programs: contract assets arise when revenue is recognized for equipment sold with promotional discounts or trade-in credits, to be amortized over the service contract term. Notes receivable are recorded when devices are sold at full price with unconditional rights to consideration--i.e., when the device is not discounted. (See page 103: "when installment sales include promotional discounts...the difference...is recorded as a contract asset...When the devices are not discounted and our right to consideration is unconditional...is recorded as a note receivable.")

AT&T recognizes revenue from customer installment payment programs at the point of sale by recording the entire amount of revenue allocated to the customer receivable (net of the fair value of any applicable trade‐in right guarantee). In practical terms, when a customer opts for an installment program, AT&T recognizes the full revenue upfront even though cash may be received over time. The accounting treatment of the difference between the recognized revenue and the actual cash received depends on the terms of the device sale:

1. If there are no promotional discounts and the customer's right to consideration is unconditional (i.e., no further performance conditions), the difference is recorded as a note receivable. This reflects an unconditional right to collect the additional amount over the installment term, and no further adjustments need to be made beyond standard credit risk and collection assessments.

2. If the installment sale includes promotional discounts that are earned over the term of the contract (for example, 'buy one get one free' or discounts contingent on ongoing service usage), the difference is recorded as a contract asset. In this case, as the promotional discounts are earned over the contract term, the contract asset is amortized over that period, reflecting the gradual recognition of the associated discount as revenue is effectively reduced over time.

In summary, the key implication is that the classification of the difference affects how future cash flows and revenue adjustments are handled. A note receivable signals an unconditional claim on cash with less complexity regarding future revenue recognition, whereas a contract asset requires systematic amortization, thereby reflecting ongoing performance obligations and the deferred adjustment of revenue over the contract term.
